results.finding: In tricyclic antidepressant poisoning, a QRS duration over 100 ms is associated with seizures and over 160 ms with ventricular arrhythmia.
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is used for QRS widening over 100 ms or ventricular arrhythmia in tricyclic poisoning.
Phenytoin and fosphenytoin add cardiac sodium-channel blockade and are avoided in tricyclic poisoning; benzodiazepines are first line for the seizures.
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine [Glauser_2016].

output.summary: Tricyclic poisoning with seizures is treated with benzodiazepines, and QRS widening with sodium bicarbonate; sodium-channel blocking antiseizure drugs are avoided.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Urine immunoassay positive for tricyclics and amphetamines; ethanol 0.08; pH 7.14 with lactate 10.8; CK 3120 with dipstick blood and no red cells; creatinine 1.8; potassium 5.2; sodium 134
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, toxicology screen, CK
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the toxicology screen identifies the ingested agents in an unknown pill [Brophy_2012]. CK because rhabdomyolysis follows prolonged convulsions with hyperthermia and decides the fluid management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus tachycardia 152 with QRS 128 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm and QTc 518 ms
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG: QRS duration, terminal R in aVR and QTc
action_criteria.rationale: A wide QRS identifies sodium-channel blocker cardiotoxicity, which needs sodium bicarbonate and rules out fosphenytoin [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Persistent coma after convulsive SE needs EEG to detect subtle or non-convulsive seizures; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step [Glauser_2016].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use phenytoin or fosphenytoin: they add sodium-channel blockade and worsen QRS prolongation and conduction.
Do not use class IA, IC or III antiarrhythmics: additive cardiac toxicity with the tricyclic.
Do not give flumazenil: it can precipitate seizures with tricyclic co-ingestion.
Do not give physostigmine for the anticholinergic features: seizures, bradycardia and asystole in tricyclic poisoning.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Give IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg as a bolus for the QRS of 128 ms, repeated until the QRS narrows, aiming for a serum pH of about 7.45-7.55, with sodium and potassium monitoring and a repeat ECG.
Secure the airway (GCS 3, SpO2 90%) and ventilate to correct the respiratory acidosis, which worsens tricyclic cardiotoxicity.
Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), or phenobarbital, and avoid fosphenytoin because it adds sodium-channel blockade to the tricyclic cardiotoxicity [ESETT_2019].
Cool actively for the temperature of 39.6 C, with benzodiazepine sedation for agitation and rigidity [Boyer_2005].
Give IV isotonic fluids for rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury (CK 3120, creatinine 1.8), with urine output, potassium, creatinine and CK monitoring.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Discuss management with a toxicologist or the poison center, and keep continuous cardiac monitoring.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
An ambulatory Holter adds nothing: the conduction toxicity is on the 12-lead ECG, and inpatient telemetry is part of management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

differential.diagnosis: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning without an MDMA contribution
differential.key_features: The wide QRS with terminal R in aVR and the positive tricyclic screen show tricyclic toxicity, but the positive amphetamine screen, hyperthermia 39.6 C and sodium 134 show an MDMA contribution
Hyperthermia, hyponatremia and the amphetamine screen fit, but MDMA does not cause a QRS of 128 ms with a terminal R in aVR
MDMA with a serotonergic tricyclic, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia and rigidity; overlaps with the toxidrome and is treated within the same plan (benzodiazepines, cooling)

differential.diagnosis: Diphenhydramine or other sodium-channel blocking anticholinergic ingestion
differential.key_features: Diphenhydramine causes seizures, mydriasis, tachycardia and QRS widening and can give a false-positive tricyclic immunoassay; the ECG management is the same, and confirmation needs quantitative serum testing
Also widens the QRS and causes hyperthermia and seizures, but the cocaine metabolite screen is negative
Temperature 39.6 C and WBC 16.4 are explained by the toxidrome and convulsions, with a clear toxicological cause and a normal CT

key_clinical_evidence: Tricyclic poisoning causes sodium-channel cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, terminal R in aVR) treated with sodium bicarbonate
Phenytoin and fosphenytoin are contraindicated in tricyclic poisoning: they worsen cardiac sodium-channel block
MDMA adds serotonergic, hyperthermic and rhabdomyolytic features
Acidosis worsens tricyclic cardiotoxicity, so ventilation and alkalinization matter

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Garcia is a 19-year-old college freshman with no medical history who is brought by EMS from a college party where he was found convulsing continuously for approximately 15 minutes. His friends report he ingested an unknown pill approximately 60-90 minutes before the seizure onset — they believe it may have been sold as 'Molly' (MDMA) but acknowledge they are not certain what it was. He had also consumed approximately 4-5 alcoholic drinks during the evening. He has absolutely no prior history of seizures. He has no medical conditions and takes no medications. On EMS arrival he was in continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity with severe agitation and hyperthermia. Temperature on EMS arrival was 39.6°C.
